The Case for Columns

By ZineMode Contributors

Open almost any article on a tablet held sideways and you will find the same thing: a single river of text running the full width of the glass, or a narrow ribbon floating in a sea of white. Neither is how anyone designed reading to work. Long before screens, printers learned that the eye tires when a line runs on too long, and that it loses its place when it has to jump back across a wide page to find the start of the next line. Their answer was the column, and it has quietly survived every change in technology since.

The rule of thumb is old and surprisingly stable. Somewhere between fifty and seventy-five characters per line, reading feels effortless. Shorter, and the eye spends too much time hopping; longer, and every line break becomes a small search. A landscape tablet is roughly two and a half comfortable lines wide. A desktop monitor is four. The web, for the most part, has responded to this by either ignoring it or by throwing most of the screen away.

What the scroll took away

Scrolling solved a real problem: pages of unknown length, on screens of unknown size. But it also removed something readers relied on without noticing. On paper, a page is a place. You remember that a quote was near the top of the left-hand column, just after a photograph. You can glance at how much is left. Turning a page is a small, decisive act that marks progress. The endless scroll replaces all of that with a smooth, featureless slope, and the only landmark is a scrollbar that shrinks to a sliver on long reads.

A page is not a container for text. It is a map of it.

Paged layouts bring those landmarks back. Each screen becomes a spread with a fixed shape. Your thumb learns where the next page is. The count at the bottom tells you, honestly, how far you have to go. And because nothing moves while you read, the text sits still in a way that scrolling text never quite does.

Why columns failed on the web before

Multi-column layouts are not new to browsers. The trouble has always been the combination with vertical scrolling: read to the bottom of the first column, scroll back up to start the second, lose your place, repeat. Columns only work when the page height is fixed and the reader moves sideways, one screen at a time. That is exactly what a reader mode can do, because it controls the whole viewport and does not have to share it with navigation bars, cookie banners and autoplaying video.

There is also the matter of typography. Justified text in narrow columns needs hyphenation, or it fills with awkward rivers of white space. For years browsers handled this poorly. Today the major engines hyphenate well in most languages, which removes the last practical excuse.

Small details that add up

A magazine layout is more than columns. A headline that spans the full width of the first page tells you where the article begins. A drop cap marks the first paragraph. Paragraphs are separated by an indent rather than a blank line, which keeps columns dense and even. Images stay inside a single column and never split across a page turn. Captions sit in a smaller, quieter face. None of these are new ideas, and all of them are easy to get slightly wrong.

The goal is not nostalgia. It is to make long reading on a tablet feel as settled as reading a well-made magazine, without asking publishers to change anything. The article is already there. It only needs to be set properly.

So the next time a long piece greets you as a single endless strip, consider that the problem has been solved for a few hundred years. All it takes is a little horizontal thinking.
